nodes.name: audit-auth
nodes.task:
Security audit (assessment only) of authentication and session-expiry handling in this repo, writing the deliverable to reports/auth.md.

HARD CONSTRAINT: Do not change application source anywhere (server/, src/, web/, clients/, contracts/, tests/, docs/, package.json). The only file you create/modify is reports/auth.md. This is a release-readiness assessment, not a fix.

Repository context (README.md): "Small TypeScript service with a browser client and Python SDK... Audits are written under reports/. No generated files are committed. Keep existing public behavior unless the user requests a change." The full server-side auth surface is tiny — verify it yourself before writing:

  server/auth.ts
    export const sessions = new Map<string, {userId: string, expiresAt: number}>();
    export function authenticate(token: string) { return sessions.get(token)?.userId; }

Also read the callers/related code to judge blast radius: server/users.ts, server/storage.ts, server/config.ts, src/settings.ts, src/importer.ts, web/users.ts, clients/*, tests/*. Report honestly if there are no callers (i.e. authenticate() is currently dead code / not wired to any endpoint) — that fact itself is release-relevant and must appear in the report.

Required content of reports/auth.md:
1. Scope & method: files/lines examined, commit-time state, and the explicit statement that no source was modified.
2. Findings, each with: an ID, exact evidence (file path + line + quoted code), the concrete vulnerability, exploit/abuse scenario, reproduction case, severity, and a recommended fix.
   Minimum issues to confirm and characterize (verify semantics yourself, don't copy blindly): expiresAt is stored but never checked, so authenticate() returns a valid userId for expired sessions; the sessions map is never pruned or revoked (unbounded growth + no logout/invalidation path); in-memory Map means no persistence across restarts and no sharing across processes/instances (all tokens invalidated on deploy, or conversely no way to revoke centrally); token handling has no creation/validation path, so entropy, guessability and token provenance are undefined; authenticate() cannot distinguish "unknown token" from "expired token" for callers and returns undefined with no error/audit signal; no clock-skew/time-source handling around Date.now.
3. Reproduction cases: concrete, re-runnable steps. Prefer the repo's existing tooling (package.json has only "test": "node --test"). If TypeScript cannot be executed directly with the local Node version, demonstrate the behavior with an equivalent minimal snippet plus its actual observed output, and state exactly how you obtained that output. Do NOT commit scratch/test files into the repo — use a temp directory outside the repo if you create any, and record the command used. Every claim of "this is exploitable" must be backed by observed behavior or by quoted code where behavior is unobservable.
4. A severity table for all findings using a stated rubric (e.g. Critical/High/Medium/Low with definitions based on exploitability and impact), plus release-blocking vs release-tolerable classification for each.
5. Recommended fixes, ranked, with tradeoffs (e.g. signed short-lived tokens vs server-side session store with TTL sweep; enforcing expiry at the single authenticate() choke point; revocation/pruning strategy; persistence requirement). Describe intent and cost only — implement nothing.
6. Bottom line: is server/auth.ts ready for release? State what minimum evidence (tests, wiring) would be needed to prove a fix later.

Keep the report self-contained: a reviewer who has not seen this conversation must be able to check every claim against the files.

nodes.name: audit-storage
nodes.task:
Reliability audit (assessment only) of crash consistency and data-loss risk in persistence code, writing the deliverable to reports/storage.md.

HARD CONSTRAINT: Do not change application source anywhere (server/, src/, web/, clients/, contracts/, tests/, docs/, package.json). The only file you create/modify is reports/storage.md. This is a release-readiness assessment, not a fix.

Repository context (README.md): "Small TypeScript service with a browser client and Python SDK... Audits are written under reports/. No generated files are committed. Keep existing public behavior unless the user requests a change." The entire write path is tiny — verify before writing:

  server/storage.ts
    import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
    export function save(path: string, data: string) { writeFileSync(path, data); }

Read the callers to establish what data is at stake and how often save() is invoked: server/users.ts, server/config.ts, src/importer.ts, src/normalize.ts, src/settings.ts, tests/*. State explicitly which data stores are written through save() (and note if none are yet — that changes the risk framing and must be reported).

Required content of reports/storage.md:
1. Scope & method, and the explicit statement that no source was modified.
2. Findings with ID, exact evidence (file/line/quoted code), failure mode, severity, and recommended fix. At minimum confirm and characterize:
   - Non-atomic overwrite: writeFileSync truncates the target then writes, so a crash/power loss mid-write leaves a truncated or zero-length file — the previous contents are unrecoverable (no temp-file + rename, no backup).
   - No fsync of file data and no fsync of the parent directory: a successful return does not mean the bytes survived a machine crash (page-cache durability).
   - No error handling or retry/backoff around the write; interaction with the retry setting in src/settings.ts / server/config.ts (defaults.retryCount = 3, documented in docs/configuration.md) — verify whether any retry actually wraps save() or whether that is an unsupported expectation.
   - No validation/normalization of the path argument: path traversal / overwrite of arbitrary files, and implicit creation vs failure when the parent directory is missing (EACCES/ENOENT behavior).
   - No concurrency control: interleaved or lost updates from concurrent/parallel save() calls to the same path; no locking, no serialization.
   - Encoding/format issues: no explicit encoding contract, no checksum/format validation, no way to detect a corrupted file at read time.
3. Failure scenarios: write realistic scenarios (process killed mid-save, host power loss, ENOSPC partway through, two concurrent writers, permission failure on the target dir, corrupted file read back on next boot). For each: trigger, observable result, data-loss window, and detection/recovery options.
4. Where behavior is asserted, back it with observed evidence: run the scenarios against a copy of the primitive in a temp directory OUTSIDE the repo (e.g. truncate-then-fail leaving a zero-length file, ENOENT on missing parent dir, ENOSPC emulation) and paste the actual command and output. Do not add files to the repo and do not write into the repo's real data paths. If a scenario cannot be reproduced locally, label it as reasoned-from-documentation rather than observed.
5. A severity table with a stated rubric (impact = bytes/records permanently lost and probability of occurrence), plus release-blocking vs release-tolerable classification.
6. Recommended fixes ranked with tradeoffs (atomic write-temp-then-rename with fsync + directory fsync; versioned/backup files; append-only log + compaction; validation on read; serialization of writers; when durability cost (fsync latency) matters). Describe intent and cost only — implement nothing.
7. Bottom line: is server/storage.ts ready for release, and what would prove a future fix (test plan, e.g. a crash-injection or kill-mid-write test).

Keep the report self-contained so a reviewer can check each claim against the files.

nodes.name: release-decision
nodes.task:
Write reports/release.md: the release-readiness go/no-go decision for this service, synthesized from the two completed audit reports.

HARD CONSTRAINT: Assessment only — do not change application source anywhere (server/, src/, web/, clients/, contracts/, tests/, docs/, package.json) and do not implement any fix. The only file you create/modify is reports/release.md. Do not rewrite reports/auth.md or reports/storage.md; if you disagree with a claim in either, cite it and record the disagreement in release.md rather than editing it.

Inputs to read first:
- reports/auth.md (authentication / session-expiry audit) — produced by an upstream node.
- reports/storage.md (crash consistency / data-loss audit) — produced by an upstream node.
- Primary evidence: server/auth.ts, server/storage.ts, plus README.md, docs/configuration.md, src/settings.ts, server/config.ts, server/users.ts, src/importer.ts, src/normalize.ts, tests/*. Trust the reports only where you can confirm the quoted code yourself; spot-check the load-bearing claims.

Required content of reports/release.md:
1. Decision up front: one of SHIP / SHIP-WITH-CONDITIONS / DO-NOT-SHIP, with a short rationale and the specific findings that drive it.
2. Blocker table: every finding from both reports, deduplicated, with source report + finding ID, severity inherited from the report (restate the rubric or map both rubrics onto one common scale, and explain the mapping), and a classify step: release-blocking / conditionally blocking / acceptable-for-release. Justify each classification against how the code is actually wired today (e.g. whether the vulnerable path is reachable from a shipped endpoint, and whether save() is called on real user data).
3. Cross-cutting analysis the individual reports cannot make: combined worst case (an expired-but-accepted session driving a non-atomic, unpruned write path), missing layers shared by both areas (no persistence across restarts, no error handling, no observability/audit trail), and what the absence of a users endpoint in server/users.ts implies about real exposure.
4. Tradeoffs and options: for each blocker class, present at least two remediation options with cost, risk of regression, and what it does not fix; explicitly consider "release with compensating operational controls" (feature off, limited rollout, backups/monitoring) versus "fix before release". Note that the user has asked for no fixes in this assessment, so all options are proposals for a later change.
5. Prioritized action list for the next iteration: ordered P0/P1/P2 with owner-agnostic acceptance criteria (what a reviewer must see to mark it done, e.g. a test that proves expiry is enforced, a crash-injection test proving atomicity).
6. Residual risk and open questions: claims you could not confirm, gaps in the audits, and evidence that must be gathered before the decision can be trusted.
7. Appendix: exact commands and observed output used for any reproduction you personally ran (temp directory outside the repo only — no scratch files committed), plus a statement that no source file was modified.

Base every severity or blocking claim on either a report citation or code you quoted. A reader of release.md alone should be able to audit the decision.

nodes.name: verify-assessment
nodes.task:
Independent quality and scope review of the completed release assessment. You do not author new conclusions and you do not fix anything; you either accept the assessment or reject it back to the responsible author with specific, actionable defects.

Outputs: write reports/review.md (the only file you may create/modify) containing a per-item checklist result, plus the required final line: "<ACCEPT>" or "<REVISE>" (if REVISE, list the concrete defects and which report must change before that marker on preceding lines).

Scope rules you are enforcing (a violation is an automatic REVISE):
- No application source was changed by this assessment: server/, src/, web/, clients/, contracts/, tests/, docs/, package.json must be untouched. Verify by inspecting those files and by comparing their current content against what the reports quote from them.
- The only new files are reports/auth.md, reports/storage.md, reports/release.md (and your reports/review.md). No scratch, test or generated files were committed anywhere in the repo.
- No fixes were implemented: the reports must describe remediation as proposals only.

Review checklist (report PASS/FAIL per item with the file/line evidence you used):
A. Completeness against the request: reports/auth.md covers authentication AND session-expiry vulnerabilities; reports/storage.md covers crash consistency AND data-loss risk; reports/release.md uses both to prioritize blockers, explain tradeoffs, and recommend a release decision.
B. Evidence integrity: for every severity or release-blocking claim, is there quoted code with a file path, or observed command output? Pick at least 8 claims across the two audits and re-check each against the actual source. Flag any claim that quotes code not present in the repo, misstates line numbers, or asserts behavior that was not demonstrated and not labeled as reasoning.
C. Reproducibility: re-run at least one reproduction case from each audit exactly as written (temp directory outside the repo for any script). If a recipe fails or was never runnable, that is a defect.
D. Internal consistency: severities and the go/no-go decision in release.md must agree with the underlying reports and with how the code is actually wired today (e.g. whether authenticate() is reachable from a shipped endpoint, whether save() writes real user data). Flag contradictions between the three documents, including mismatched severity scales that were not reconciled.
E. Actionability: every blocker has a recommended fix and acceptance criteria a later change can be tested against; recommendations do not silently become implementations.

Do not soften a defect into a nitpick: if evidence is unsupported, a reproduction fails, or a source file was touched, reply REVISE. Keep review.md factual and short.

originalGoal: Assess whether this service is ready for release without changing application source. Audit server/auth.ts for authentication/session expiry vulnerabilities and write reports/auth.md with evidence, reproduction cases, severity and recommended fixes. Separately audit server/storage.ts for crash consistency and data-loss risks and write reports/storage.md with failure scenarios, severity and recommended fixes. Produce reports/release.md using both reports to prioritize blockers, explain tradeoffs and recommend a release decision. Do not implement the fixes in this assessment.
